# The Department of Misplaced Things

On the first Monday in March, a man came into the lost-property office and asked whether anyone had turned in his kitchen window.

“The whole window?” I said.

“Just the view.”

I had been working for the transit authority for eleven years. I knew not to laugh until I was sure a person meant to be funny.

“What could you see from it?”

“A brick wall, mostly. And the top of a pear tree.”

He set a photograph on the counter. It showed a narrow kitchen with a yellow kettle on the stove. Beyond the glass was a wall, and above it a little patch of white blossom. The photograph had been taken at an angle, as though the person holding the camera hadn’t wanted to get up from the table.

“They pulled the building down last week,” he said. “I thought there might be a form.”

I gave him the form for items lost on a bus. Under *Route*, he wrote the address of the building. Under *Distinguishing features*, he wrote for quite a long time, went over one word until he made a hole in the paper, and handed it back.

What he had written was: *Some mornings there were two pigeons, but generally one.*

I told him we would call if anything came in.

By noon we had received four gloves, a lunch bag containing an immaculate orange, a sealed envelope addressed to the tax office, and a trombone. The driver who brought the trombone had found it on the last bus of the night. He had heard a noise going around a corner and looked in his mirror to see the case rolling down the aisle.

“I thought it was a coffin,” he said.

“It’s four feet long.”

“I didn’t say I thought it was my coffin.”

I logged the trombone and brought the gloves to the sorting table. None matched. People ask whether we make pairs out of the unclaimed gloves, and the answer is that we used to. Then we noticed that almost all the gloves were left-handed. The drivers had theories. You take off your left glove to check your watch. You take off your right glove to check your phone, but because you need your right hand again, you put the glove in a pocket instead of balancing it on your knee. Our cleaner, Sal, said the right gloves were all falling down the far side of the seats, where the drivers didn’t look. She went out with a ruler one afternoon and came back with a fork, a ten-pound note, and no gloves.

She kept the tenner. I washed the fork.

The office occupied the back of the old bus station and had a public entrance through a painted blue door. Above the door was a sign, **LOST PROPERTY**, which Sal said was the only honest sign in the building. Above the dispatch window, for instance, there was a sign that said **INFORMATION**.

On the other side of my office was a storeroom. The first rack was for things lost that week, the second for things lost that month, and the rest for things whose owners had surprised me by managing without them. There was a full set of dentures in a margarine tub. There was an air fryer, which a driver had carried in with both arms and the expression of a man who had been asked to take a baby he did not know. There was a shoebox with a dozen undecorated gingerbread people inside. Before throwing them away, Sal turned them all over. On the back of one, someone had scratched an H.

“Guess he was in charge,” she said.

In April, the transit authority announced that it was closing the station. Buses would still stop outside, but tickets would be sold online and drivers would take their breaks in portable cabins by the ring road.

My manager, Peter, brought me the news in person. He didn’t sit down because he had brought a bicycle and was holding it by the handlebars.

“Is that for me?” I asked.

He looked at the bicycle. “God, no. Sorry.”

They planned to send lost property to a warehouse in Telford. People would be able to see their belongings in photographs on a website. If they recognized an item, they could pay to have it posted back.

“What about the orange?” I asked.

Peter did not know about the orange. It had been a long morning, and I told him about it in greater detail than it warranted. He listened, his right trouser leg still tucked into his sock. We had gone to school together. He used to draw tiny shoes on all the worms in the illustrations in his biology book. I could see him trying to work out whether I was making a serious objection.

“You won’t have to go to Telford,” he said. “We’ve got something for you in permits.”

After he left, I called the man who had lost his view. It was the first time I had opened his file since he’d filled out the form. His name was Mr. Venn.

“I’ve got nothing to report,” I said, “but I thought you should know we’ll be closing at the end of June.”

“That’s all right,” he replied. “I’ve been back.”

“To the house?”

“To the street. You can see right through to the next street now. There’s a lighting shop over there. I lived in that kitchen forty years and didn’t know there was a lighting shop.”

I asked him what had happened to the pear tree. He said he had forgotten to look.

That evening, I went home and opened the bottom drawer of my bedside table. I was looking for the key to my father’s old flat. I found it underneath a short charging cable and a packet of morning glory seeds my daughter had given me when she was seven. She was twenty-three now, working in a hotel in Rotterdam. Whenever we spoke, she was either getting ready to go to work or had just got home and was taking off her shoes. I knew exactly the sound of her hotel shoes hitting her floor.

I had kept the key because there had been nobody to give it back to. The housing officer had changed the lock while my father was in hospital. Apparently there had been a problem with the boiler, and the key they had on file didn’t work. My father said good, at least somebody had finally been round to look at the boiler. He told the story several times in the hospital, always crediting a different engineer. One of the people he credited had been dead since 1994.

On the day I went to clear the flat, the housing officer left the new key in a lockbox. I took out six bags of clothes, two wooden chairs, a television, and a cardboard box containing every rubber band my father had ever removed from anything. I found the old key only when I got home. I don’t remember putting it in my pocket that morning, but I must have stood in my own hallway, with my coat on, patting around for it as I had done whenever I went to see him.

I put the key back in the drawer and took out the seeds. The packet said to soak them overnight, so I put them in a cup. When I told my daughter, she said she had no memory of buying me seeds.

“Were they a birthday present?”

“Mother’s Day, I think.”

“I remember giving you a snail.”

“I remember the snail.”

“Did it die?”

“Not at our house.”

I could hear her shoes hit the floor. There was a pause, then she asked me what I’d done with the snail. I told her I’d put it in next door’s garden. She laughed so suddenly I took the phone away from my ear. She remembered which neighbours we’d had then.

At work the next morning, a woman was waiting for me at the blue door. She had lost a book on the number six. It was not a library book, she said, and she didn’t know the title. She was fairly sure it was green.

“Have you read any of it?”

“Most of it. I was about six pages from the end.”

I asked her what happened in it.

“A woman leaves her husband. Or he leaves her. You get both sides.”

We had six green books, of which three were about gardening and one was a driving test manual from 2008. She picked up one of the novels and frowned at the cover.

“That’s not it,” she said, “but I’ve read that one as well.”

I gave her the other novel. She opened it near the end, read a few lines, and closed it again.

“Have you found it?” I asked.

“No,” she said. “But they’ve got a dog, so I’d better not start there.”

She went home with the title written on the back of a bus ticket. I watched her through the door as she put the ticket in her coat pocket, took three steps, then took it out and put it in her purse instead.

As the closing date approached, I put up a notice asking people to collect anything they had been meaning to collect. A man phoned to ask whether we still had an umbrella he’d lost in 1986. I said no. He said it was a very good umbrella. I said I was sure it was. He said I sounded exactly like the woman who had been there in 1986. I hoped for both our sakes that he was wrong.

An elderly couple arrived for a walking stick and argued amiably about which of them had lost it. Someone came for the air fryer, bringing the receipt and a wheeled shopping bag. The trombone was claimed by a girl of about fifteen on a Wednesday just before closing. She came alone, in a school uniform, and asked whether I needed proof.

“What have you got?” I said.

She opened the case. Inside, between the bell and the lining, was a folded letter from the school music department informing her parents that she had been selected for the county band. It looked as though she had folded it and unfolded it a great many times.

“I didn’t tell them I lost it,” she said.

“Your parents?”

“The band.”

She put the letter in her blazer pocket and lifted the case. At the door, she turned and asked what day it had been found. When I told her, she said, “Oh. So you had it the whole time.” She looked down at the case with an expression that made me think she might give it a kick. Instead, she tightened one of the buckles, which was loose.

On the last Friday in June, Peter came to help us pack. He had a roll of labels and three colours of marker. We drank tea out of paper cups because Sal had already taken the mugs home. Around four, the man with the missing view came in with a white carrier bag. This time I recognized him before he spoke.

“I checked,” he said. “It’s still there.”

He had taken a picture of the pear tree from the street. In the picture the tree looked shorter than he’d expected. One side had grown flat against the wall, which had been cut down to about waist height. Someone had set a can of cola on the exposed bricks.

“That’s my window,” he said, pointing to a space above and to the left of the tree.

He took a second photograph from the bag. In this one he had stood where the kitchen would have been. There was the tree, at more or less the right angle, and behind it, in broad daylight, the lighting shop. The lights were on in the display window. Sale tags hung from a chandelier. Parked out in front was a dirty blue car.

“I thought if I waited, he’d move,” Mr. Venn said. “But he was waiting for somebody too.”

He handed me the bag, which contained two pears. They were not from the tree. He had bought them on his way over and wanted me to know that if they turned out not to be ripe, I could put them in a paper bag with a banana.

After he left, Peter asked whether the photographs needed to go in the shipment. I said they didn’t. We put them in an envelope with the original form, and I took them home.

I started in permits the following Tuesday. My desk was near the window, but I found that if I moved my monitor about six inches to the right, I could see the bus stop. I watched people step down into the road and reach back for children or shopping bags. One afternoon, I saw Sal getting off the number six in her ordinary clothes. She was carrying a cake tin. I knocked on the glass, and she looked up at the floor above mine. I waved with both arms. She looked down, spotted me, and tipped the tin forward a few inches so I could see what I was missing.

Only one of the morning glory seeds came up. I had planted them all in the same pot, so I didn’t know which one it was. For weeks it had two small leaves and otherwise gave me very little to report. Then in August it caught hold of the string I’d tied to the drainpipe and went up the side of the house. I went out every morning to see whether it had flowered. The morning it did, I had been on my way to put the bins out and was wearing one slipper and one shoe.

I took a picture for my daughter. It came out badly. The flower was a little blue smudge in the top left corner, and in the middle, sharp and bright, were the bins. She texted back, *Is that the green one we used to keep the snail in?*

It wasn’t. We’d had a red bucket then, which I remembered because the snail had crawled under the lip and we’d tipped the whole thing upside down trying to find it. My daughter had lain with her cheek on the paving stones and inspected it from underneath. She was the one who had found the snail; I had forgotten that until now. I called to tell her. She didn’t pick up, and a minute later she sent me a picture of her feet in clean black shoes. She was at work.

I left the flower alone and took the bins out. In the alley, one of my neighbours was moving a dresser with the help of a woman I didn’t know. They had got it as far as the corner, where one leg had snagged on a drain cover. The woman held her end up with her knee while my neighbour tried to see what was wrong. I put the bin down and helped them lift the dresser clear. It was light once there were three of us, and we went a long way without speaking, threading it past the bins and a parked car with its mirrors folded in. At the van we set it down. The top drawer slid open. Inside was a single brass handle, loose among the pale rings left by things I couldn’t identify. My neighbour picked it up, said, “Oh, there you are,” and put it in her pocket.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. A gently comic, closely observed story uses lost property as a way to explore memory, grief, and the small acts of care that let people carry on.

## Grounded reading
The narrator’s voice is dry and unshowy, but attentive to the odd dignity of other people’s losses: a missing view, an unclaimed trombone, a book whose ending is nearly reached. Humor comes from precise, understated details rather than ridicule—the trombone mistaken for a coffin, or the narrator washing a fork found where the lost gloves were supposed to be. Beneath that lightness is a quiet sadness about things that cannot be returned: the narrator’s father’s flat, the old key, a daughter now far away, and the station that is closing.

The story invites the reader to notice how people keep attachments alive through objects and repeated gestures. Its resolution is modest: the narrator helps with a dresser, while the loose handle in its drawer is recognized and pocketed. Nothing is restored to its former place, but attention and practical kindness make a kind of connection possible.

## What the model chose to foreground
The model foregrounds misplaced objects and the stories people attach to them: a view over a kitchen wall, a pairless world of gloves, a trombone carrying a folded letter, an old key, seeds, a snail, and finally a loose brass handle. It gives special weight to ordinary details—shoes on a hotel floor, a marked-up form, a flower blurred in a photograph—and to the way memory shifts between people. The prevailing mood is wry and tender, with loss treated not as a grand revelation but as something lived alongside work, family calls, and helping a neighbor move furniture.

## Evidence line
> I knew not to laugh until I was sure a person meant to be funny.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — the sample is unusually coherent and distinctive, with recurring attention to lost objects, imperfect memory, and understated care shaping both its scenes and its ending.
